title: Ice sheet expansion may have started 2,000 years ago, but we canceled that
gist: A Science study led by Nicolás Young (Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory) uses beryllium-10 exposure dating and radiocarbon kill dates of moss from under the cold-based Barnes Ice Cap, the last remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, to show the ice reached its minimum about 3,600 years ago and began re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, the start of the next glaciation. Human-driven CO2 rises reversed that advance by about 1960; Barnes now has no accumulation zone and will vanish within a few centuries, and Young argues greenhouse gases have ended one of Earth's most regular cycles.

insights.claim: A Science study finds the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest size about 3,600 years ago and began re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, which the researchers interpret as the opening move of the next glaciation.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: It reframes the pre-industrial climate baseline as one already trending toward glaciation.

insights.claim: Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island is the last surviving fragment of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, which at its peak buried most of Canada under two miles of ice and held about 80 meters of sea level.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Shows how much sea-level change ice-sheet cycles involve.
insights.locator: Barnes Ice Cap sits on the central plateau

insights.claim: About 70 percent of the moss radiocarbon dates cluster around 1800 CE, the peak of the Little Ice Age, which Young treats as one late pulse within an advance that had run for two thousand years.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Recasts the Little Ice Age as part of a longer cooling trend rather than a standalone event.
insights.locator: About 70 percent of the team’s radiocarbon dates

insights.claim: Nearly 200 kill dates from neighboring small ice caps on the same plateau include none older than 2,000 years, which Young takes to mean they, and probably Barnes, all began advancing about 2,000 years ago.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Regional consistency firms up the timing of the turnaround.
insights.quote: all of those ice caps up there didn’t start advancing or re-expanding until about 2,000 years ago

themes.theme: How a cold-based ice cap keeps its record

insights.claim: Barnes is cold-based, meaning frozen to the bedrock so it cannot slide; unlike warm-based glaciers, which slide on meltwater and grind away what lies beneath, it preserved tundra plants it smothered in place for two millennia.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Explains why this site holds a rare, intact record of when an ice sheet first turns around.

insights.claim: Beryllium-10 accumulating in exposed rock surfaces dates the retreat, showing the Laurentide had pulled back within today's ice margin by 3,600 years ago and probably further by about 3,000; radiocarbon dating of moss killed by advancing ice gives kill dates that map the readvance.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Two independent dating methods underpin the timeline.

insights.claim: Barnes' margin has retreated 200 to 800 meters since 1960, exposing mosses killed from about 1000 CE onward; Young expects further retreat within about 20 years to expose the decisive 2,000-year-old plants.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Continued melt will itself provide a direct test of the study's inferred start date.
insights.quote: If we went back there in 20 years or something, as the ice margin has retreated a little more, we actually might be able to sample those 2,000-year-old plants

insights.claim: High-latitude northern insolation peaked 10,000 to 11,000 years ago and has fallen since, while CO2 rose about 20 ppm between 8,000 and 2,000 years ago; Young says the insolation drop overwhelmed the small CO2 warming, so ice sheets began growing 2,000 years ago.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Quantifies how weak the pre-industrial CO2 forcing was compared with orbital forcing.
insights.quote: That drop in insolation and temperatures actually overwhelmed the small temperature forcing the little bit of carbon dioxide rise
insights.locator: Solar energy reaching high northern latitudes

insights.claim: Young sees no contradiction with models saying the next ice age was postponed by tens of thousands of years, because those models define glacial inception as ice reaching a large size, whereas his data catches the first turnaround of an ice sheet.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: The disagreement is about definitions, so the field result and the models can both hold.
insights.locator: A lot of people have defined glacial inception

insights.claim: Greenhouse gases rose about 12 ppm from 1750 to 1850, another 50 ppm by 1960 and a further 138 ppm by 2024; by 1960 Barnes' mass balance turned negative and its advance ended.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Dates the moment human forcing overtook orbital cooling at this site.
insights.locator: Greenhouse gases had risen by about 12 ppm

insights.claim: The share of Barnes' surface above the snow line fell from about 35 percent in the 1960s-70s to about 3 percent by the early 2000s and zero today, leaving no accumulation zone, and Young's models show it disappearing within a few centuries under any plausible emissions scenario.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Shows Arctic ice loss is locked in regardless of emissions path.
insights.quote: An ice cap or glacier cannot survive if it does not have an accumulation zone.
insights.locator: Today, Barnes Ice Cap is dying

insights.claim: Young argues greenhouse warming has not saved us from anything, since a full ice age would have taken tens of thousands of years, but it has ended the 2.5-million-year pacing of ice ages, one of the most regular cycles on Earth.
insights.speaker: Jacek Krywko
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the idea that warming staved off an ice age, and frames it instead as breaking a long-standing Earth-system cycle.
insights.quote: We have evidence now that humans, and specifically greenhouse gases, have actually terminated one of the most consistent cycles on Earth.
